cultivar: Fengqing large-leaf and other Yunnan big-leaf (assamica) cultivars
processing: Fully oxidised bud tea shaped straight: early-spring buds are withered, rolled lightly and oxidised, and at some stage straightened by hand or machine so they dry as rigid needles. The order and method vary by maker.
harvest_season: Early spring (March to early April); the straight shape needs fat, intact buds, which only the first flush gives.
appearance_dry: Slim, straight, even golden needles with darker tips, looking almost like a bundle of matches.
appearance_wet: Straight copper-gold buds that stand upright in the cup before softening.
taste_profile: Honey and caramel first, then sweet potato and malt, with a cleaner, slightly mineral finish than loose Golden Buds and a touch more briskness.

brewing.notes: The needles sink slowly, so give the second steep a little longer than expected. A glass pitcher or gaiwan shows the needles standing up. Western-style: 2.5 g per 250 ml, 2.5–3 minutes.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, usually with the county named. It is a drink-within-a-year tea, not one to age.
description:
Yunnan Golden Needle, Dian Hong Jin Zhen, is the straightened, tidied cousin of Golden Buds: the same early-spring buds from Yunnan's big-leaf bushes, shaped into slim, straight, golden needles instead of being left loose and curly. Fengqing in Lincang, the home of Dian Hong, is the place most often named for it.

Beyond withering, a light roll, oxidation and drying, the buds are straightened by hand or machine so they dry rigid and uniform; methods vary by maker. Many drinkers find Jin Zhen brews a touch darker and brisker than loose Jin Ya.

In the cup it is honey and caramel first, then sweet potato and malt, with a cleaner, slightly more mineral finish than Golden Buds and a lovely golden-orange colour. Keep the water around 90 °C and the first steeps short; the needles sink slowly, so give the second steep a bit longer than you would expect. It is a tea that rewards a glass pitcher: watching the needles stand up is half the fun.

It is sold by the current spring, usually with the county named. The straight shape makes it easy to judge: needles should be even, plump and gold with a few darker tips, not a mix of gold and broken brown bits. 'Golden Needle' from Guangxi or Sichuan exists and can be fine, just cheaper, and it should be labelled as such.

If you like it, the Pine Needle style (Song Zhen) is the leafier, more robust straight-leaf Dian Hong.
history:
Golden Needle belongs to the family of Dian Hong, Yunnan's black tea, which itself is young. Wartime pushed the tea trade to the southwest in 1938, when Feng Shaoqiu set up a Yunnan tea company. The Shunning factory (now Fengqing) followed in March 1939 and trials began there, and the first 15 tonnes went out through Hong Kong to Britain that same year.

The needle shape came later and its date is not well documented. The Yunnan Academy of Agricultural Sciences tea institute lists Dian Hong Jin Zhen among the new products it developed, which suggests a modern research-era style rather than an old craft. Today the name describes a look, straight golden bud needles, more than one defined recipe.
